What I do with it is this. I stay. I name what I see. I refuse to pretend that the rooms I enter unhindered are the same rooms my children enter. I refuse to weaponise my own legibility into silence about everyone whose body the country has decided to read differently.
What the body already knew
The cab driver saw a name and made it mean one thing. My mother saw names and wished they meant something else. Texas saw a girl who kissed the wrong boy and did not stand for the right flag.
The world has always been making up its mind about me and about the people I love based on one signal, one name, one refusal to comply.

I have never been interested in compliance. I have been interested in presence. In what happens when a body stays. When it does not fold, does not explain itself, does not apologise for taking up space in a room that was not designed for it.
My son was seven, standing in the rain outside a black cab in London.

He looked up at me and asked what had happened. I lied to him because I was not yet ready to tell the truth. That the world would do this. That the name his father and I gave him with love and intention would, in some rooms, be the only thing people heard.
He knows now. He has always known.
The body learns before the parent explains. His body learned it that day on the pavement: the specific feeling of being expelled from a space you believed was yours.

I teach people to listen to what the body already knows. I teach them that the first signal is almost always right. I teach them that what was done to the body does not have to be the body's final word.

I was taught this by a four-year-old version of myself who saw energy. By a biology teacher in Texas who said pay attention to what you are already doing. By a boy whose name made a cab driver turn around. By a cross burning on a neighbour's lawn. By a body that moved toward what it was told to fear, every single time, and found that the thing on the other side was always more true than the warning.

I know what it is to be a parent with children in places that are dangerous and beloved. I have four children with Muslim names because I married the man I loved and gave them the names that carried his lineage. I have a life that does not fit into a single sentence because I stopped trying to make it fit.
The part you are afraid to say out loud: the name, the desire, the thing that does not match the package. I have probably already met it.
Still following the breadcrumbs.Juliette

q: What the Body Was Told

blocks.x: Part One: What I was told
I was seven years old the first time I understood that my body was not entirely mine.

He was family. The life of the party. Big hands, big ears, big laugh, the kind of man who makes a room louder just by walking into it. He especially loved the children. He chased us around gardens at family gatherings while the adults drank wine and called it wholesome.
The hugs lasted slightly too long. His hand moved somewhere it should not. Five times. The fifth time, I told my mother.
She said: “That is just what uncles do.”

Something rewired in that moment. If what felt wrong was normal, if a person who loved me could touch me in a way that made my skin want to leave my body and that was simply how uncles were, then I could not trust what I felt. My body's signal was wrong. Being seen, being a girl in a room, being noticed. None of it was safe.
I did not decide this.
My body decided it.
Part Two: The weight
From age eight, the weight began to arrive.

I did not understand what I was doing. Nobody does. The body does not explain its logic. It does not send a memo. It simply begins to build something. A layer. A buffer. A way of taking up space that, paradoxically, makes you less of a target. Less visible. Less reachable.

Research confirms what the body already knew before there were words for it. Women who experience unwanted touch in childhood are significantly more likely to carry excess weight in adulthood. The body is not malfunctioning. It is following an instruction.
Nobody asked the eight-year-old why she was getting bigger.
They just told her to eat less.
Part Three: The loud dress
I also went the other direction.

A sequin skirt that catches light from across the room. A denim jacket covered in rainbow stars and coloured stitching that no dress code could have anticipated. A feathered military hat that belongs to no era and no occasion. A hot pink dress with a print so loud it arrived somewhere before I did.
I wear things nobody else is wearing. I put combinations together that should not work, and I know, in the moment I am getting dressed, that they do. Because of how they feel.

The little frisson when the sequins touch my skin, hard and cool and slightly rough. The way feathers at a bustier's edge tickle my neck, like a lover tracing something very slowly along my jaw. The weight of a jacket settling onto my shoulders, grounding me into my own body before I have walked into a room.
This is about being inside a body I can feel.
The woman who learned to make herself invisible also learned to go numb inside the invisibility. The armour and the going quiet arrived together.
What came back, when it came back, was sensation. The scratch of sequins. The cool slide of silk. The way a print so bold you cannot look away from it somehow makes you feel most like yourself.
I love my body at every size I have been in it. It has been doing something brave the whole time. Making decisions I had not yet caught up with.
Part Four: The instruction
What I was told, and what most women I sit with were told, runs something like this.
“You would be so pretty if you just lost a little weight.”
Said by a mother who was told the same thing by her mother.

Said with love, received by the body as: you are not enough as you are. Earn your softness. Earn the right to take up space. Earn the attention, earn the touch, earn the dress you actually want to wear. After.
After the weight loss. After the discipline. After you have made yourself smaller first.
The cruelty dressed as care. The comment at the dinner table that the person who made it does not remember and the body that received it never forgot.

Underneath all of that, for so many of the women who come to me, there is something that happened before there were words for it. Something in the body that decided, below the level of conscious thought, that less visible was safer. That wanting less was wiser. That taking up space, real space, felt space, desired space, was not available to her.
Almost every woman I have worked with who carries body shame also carries something in her relationship to touch, to intimacy, to being known.
They are not separate.

The body that cannot be touched is almost always the body that learned, somewhere and from someone, that touch was not safe. Or that it was something to be endured. Or that being fully felt was dangerous.
Part Five: Three women
Let me tell you about three women.

The first came from New York. A lawyer. Successful in the way that looks, from the outside, like everything is fine. She could not gain weight, no matter what she ate, what supplements she took, what specialists examined her. Her body refused to hold.
The doctors found nothing wrong.

What we found in the work was something no doctor had a test for. She had left Ethiopia. Built a life in America. Achieved everything her family had sacrificed to make possible. Her country had known famine for decades. Generations of her people had not had enough.

Her body, carrying that history in its cells, had decided, completely, subconsciously, with total commitment, that she did not deserve to be full. To hold weight felt like a betrayal of everyone who had gone without.

You cannot talk the body out of its instructions. We worked with where it lived. Below language, in the nervous system, in the cellular memory where these things are stored. When the guilt began to move, her body began to change.
The second came from France. An aristocratic family. The kind of upbringing that has a rule for everything, including how much space a woman should take up.
Her mother had been clear. “Larger women are common.” To carry weight was low class. To be controlled, in body, in appetite, in how much you allowed yourself, was refinement. Was correct.
She had held that instruction for decades. She ate carefully, joylessly, obsessively.
Her husband was having an affair. The woman he was seeing was fuller, softer, warmer in ways his wife had been taught to refuse herself.
We worked. The grip began to loosen. The rituals around food softened. She started to eat without punishment. To feel without immediately classifying the feeling.
She and her husband went to Vietnam. A second honeymoon. Something between them had at last become spacious enough to breathe.

The third came in her forties. Just slightly absent from herself. Dressing for what fit rather than what suited her, moving through her life and her marriage like a woman who had quietly stopped arriving.
Her husband loved her. She could not quite receive it.

In our work together, something surfaced that had no clear memory attached to it. Pre-verbal. Before she had language, before she could have named it. The body had stored it below the floor of conscious memory. As an instruction. Want less. Be less here. Take up less.
She had been following that instruction for forty years without knowing it had been given.

When it began to clear, she started dressing differently. Just wearing what suited her body rather than what apologised for it. She started asking for touch differently in her bedroom. Asking for what she actually wanted.
Her husband noticed. He was, in her words, delighted.
Because she had arrived in it.
Part Six: The real question
Shame does not disappear when the body changes.

I have watched women lose significant weight and become harder. More critical of other women's bodies, harsher in their judgements. Because they remember too well. The shame stayed. It just changed direction. It turned outward instead of inward.
I have watched women discipline their bodies into thinness and still feel enormous inside it. Still feel like too much. Still dress for what fits rather than what delights them.
The body was never the trouble. The body is always responding to something.
The question worth asking, gently, in a way the nervous system can actually receive, is not how do I change this body.
It is: what was this body told, and by whom, and is any of it still true?
Because the instruction is not permanent.

The body that learned to hide can learn to feel the scratch of sequins and know it is safe to be here. The body that learned to disappear can learn to walk into a room in a feathered hat that belongs to no occasion and feel, in its bones, that this is exactly right.
Just as a body, at last, that has come home to itself.
Still following the breadcrumbs.Juliette

q: What the Body Knows When It Finally Feels Held

blocks.x: She called me from the bath.

I recognised the tone immediately. That particular quality of voice that sits somewhere between elation and confusion. The nervous system flooded. The mind trying to catch up with what the body just experienced.

She is a client. Highly aware. Trained in body-based work herself. Going through a separation. Looking, in her own words, to feel safe again: in herself, in her body, in the possibility of connection.
She had been to a networking event.
A man approached her. He was learning to be a shaman, he said. He looked at her and asked a question she was not prepared for.
How often have you been truly held?
It hit her like a ton of bricks. Her own words.
She had been going through so much. The marriage ending. The recalibration of everything she thought her life was going to look like. The question landed somewhere she had not let anyone near.
He said: there is a hotel just across the road. Come with me. I will hold you. No strings attached. Nothing more than that.
Part One: What the body did next
I want to pause here.
Because I know what happened in her body in that moment.
Oxytocin. Dopamine. The nervous system recognising, finally, the possibility of safe touch. Of being held without having to perform or manage or give anything back.

These are not small things. These are the chemicals the body is designed to release in the presence of genuine safety. Research on affectionate touch consistently shows that being held activates C-tactile fibres in the skin, triggers oxytocin release, lowers cortisol, and shifts the nervous system toward rest and connection. When you have been touch-starved, and separation does that, grief does that, years of managing everything alone does that, the flood is profound.
It is also, and this is the part nobody talks about enough, profoundly disorienting.

Research published in Frontiers in Neuroscience found that oxytocin can impair decision-making under ambiguity. It increases trust and simultaneously reduces the capacity to read risk accurately. The very chemical that makes you feel safe can, in the wrong container, make it harder to identify that you are not.
She said yes.
They sat together for hours. Her on his lap. Her body doing exactly what a body does when it finally feels held: it softened. It opened. It exhaled years of bracing.
When she asked what people around them must be thinking, he said: they think you are my wife or my girlfriend, and you are upset, and I am comforting you.
She asked what would happen if his wife saw this.
He gave what she described as a blasé remark.
They both went to the bathroom.
When they returned, he told her he had taken the liberty of booking a hotel room.
It had come through him, he said, that this was a service he needed to provide for her.
Part Two: What that sentence means
I need you to sit with that sentence for a moment.
It came through me that I need to do this service for you.
She said no. Her body said no. She felt it immediately: that contraction, that something-is-wrong signal the nervous system sends before the mind has found the words.
He said: no problem.
She relaxed again.
The oxytocin was still flooding her system. The hours of being held had done what hours of being held do. Her body had been given something it had been craving, and now it was terrified of losing it.
She changed her mind.
They had sex.
Afterwards, she told me: he had not climaxed. She had already decided this meant it had all been for her pleasure.
I have been sitting with that sentence ever since.
Where did we teach women that a man's climax is the only evidence of his pleasure? Where did we teach women that a man who does not climax has given rather than taken?
Part Three: What this actually is
This is grooming.

The Campaign Against Adult Grooming describes the pattern precisely: a person builds trust using charm, attentiveness, sensitivity, and empathy, then exploits what they have created. Groomers often claim special connections with their targets. They use mirroring, echoing back the target's own story, and frame the relationship as unique, sacred, chosen.
How often have you been truly held? is mirroring. It names her longing back to her.
It has come through me that I need to do this service for you is sacred framing. The spiritual authority used to make violation feel like blessing.

Researchers Winters and Jeglic found that in adult settings, perpetrators use love-bombing, overwhelming affirmation, to bypass critical thinking. When a person in spiritual authority employs these tactics, it can feel sacred. A person studying shamanism is positioning himself as someone with access to higher guidance. That positioning is not incidental. It is the architecture.
This is the quiet, sophisticated, devastatingly effective version that happens in wellness spaces, spiritual communities, and the places women go specifically because they are trying to heal.

This is also why so many women do not name it. The chemicals in the body said: this is what you needed. To call it otherwise feels like a betrayal of the softening they genuinely felt. So they do not name it. They just quietly stop knowing how to receive.
Part Four: What her body was actually doing
Let me name what actually happened, layer by layer.

A man in a position of perceived spiritual authority identified a woman in a vulnerable moment. He used language designed to open her, language that bypasses the thinking mind and speaks directly to the longing body. He created a container of apparent safety. He held her until her nervous system flooded with bonding hormones. He waited. He booked the room. He framed what he wanted as a spiritual calling, as service, as something that had come through him for her benefit.
The body did not betray her.
The body was doing exactly what it is designed to do.

It felt held and opened toward more holding. That is biology. What she needed to know, what so many women in that moment need to know, is that the flood of safety chemicals was real, and the source of them was not safe. Both things are true at the same time.
Part Five: What I spend my days undoing
I have spent twenty-seven years working at this exact intersection.
The nervous system that has been touch-starved will reach for the first thing that feels like nourishment. This is survival. The body is trying to get what it needs.

What I do, what ethical body-based intimacy work does, is create a container so precise that the hormones can do their work without the woman having to hand herself over to access them. The release is real. The opening is real. The safety is also real.
The distinction matters more than I have words for.

Because what happens in a room like the one she ended up in rewires something. It teaches the nervous system that opening leads to violation. That safety is a trap. That the longing itself is dangerous.
It takes what her body was correctly seeking and turns it into evidence that her body cannot be trusted.

The women who come to me years later wondering why they shut down when someone tries to hold them, why they cannot receive even with someone safe, why intimacy feels like a threat they cannot explain. Many of them, when we trace the thread back, find a room like this one. A moment where the body learned that opening leads to somewhere she did not mean to go.
This is what I work to undo. Session after session. With women who came before her and women who will come after.
Part Six: For the woman reading this
She is okay. She is processing it with the clarity of someone who has language for it.
She called it what it was. Eventually. After the chemicals settled and the confusion lifted and the quiet devastation of realising what had actually happened moved through her.
Not every woman gets there. Not every woman has the language, or the container, or the friend who picks up the phone.
I am writing this for the ones who don't.
Your body did not fail you.
It did exactly what it was designed to do in the presence of what looked like safety. The longing for touch, for holding, for being truly seen: that longing is one of the most human things about you.
Still following the breadcrumbs.Juliette

q: When the Air Has Changed

blocks.x: You said something. Or she did.
Or someone walked into the kitchen at the wrong moment. Or a name came up that should not have.
Whatever it was, the air between you has changed.

You can feel it without looking. Her body has gone still in a way that is louder than her voice. Yours has gone tight in a way she will be reading even though neither of you is looking at the other. Both of you are waiting for the other one to do something. Neither of you knows what.
The room is not quiet. The room is full of everything that just happened.
This is the moment most men freeze.
I want to walk you through what is actually happening between you. Then I want to tell you what works.
Her body has already shifted state, before either of you said a word
A man wrote me a message last week. He did not include details. He did not ask for advice. He said, plainly: I do not know how to be with her after something hard has been said. I freeze.
He is not the first.

It is one of the most common questions I get from men, and one of the least answered. There is endless content about how to set the scene. How to flirt. How to lead. How to initiate. There is almost nothing on what to do with the air after something has already been said.
So here is what is happening on her side.

When something has just landed in her body that her system has read as threat, your tone, the look on your face, a phrase that hit something it did not know was sore, her nervous system has done what it has been doing since long before she met you. It has shifted state.

Stephen Porges, whose Polyvagal Theory has been the foundational map for two decades of trauma work, would describe what happened as a move from ventral vagal, the social engagement state where conversation and real listening are biologically possible, into either sympathetic activation or dorsal collapse.
In the first, her body has prepared to fight or flee. In the second, it has gone still and far away. The face you are looking at is no longer the face you were having dinner with five minutes ago.
Most importantly, she is not deciding to be like this.

Her body has done it for her. The decision happened in milliseconds, before language arrived. She is now living inside a state her body produced as protection. Trying to reach her with words at this point is like trying to call across a canyon. She can hear sound. She cannot quite reach the meaning.

If you have ever asked her in this state what do you need from me right now and watched her face go blanker, this is why. Her access to language and connection has briefly gone offline. Asking for one is asking for something her system cannot produce.
The body has to come back first.
You are in the same state. A different shape of it
Here is the part nobody tells you.

When you saw her face change, your nervous system did its own scan. The signal it picked up was almost certainly some version of: I am about to lose her, or I am about to be in trouble, or I have just done something I cannot undo.
Your body responded the way it learned to respond a long time ago. Maybe at three. Maybe at seven. The age is different for every man. The pattern is consistent.

Some men go into fixing mode. The mind starts running options. The body leans forward. Words begin pouring out, all of them aimed at making her face soften. The fixing is not coming from connection. It is coming from a body trying to switch off an alarm.
She can feel the difference. It does not land as care. It lands as pressure.

Some men go cold. The body pulls back. Walls go up that were rehearsed in a childhood when reaching out got punished. The face goes neutral. The voice flattens. It looks like calm. It is dorsal vagal collapse, the same state hers may have just entered, in a different shape.

Some men go hot. Anger arrives almost instantly, often surprising them with how fast. Underneath the anger is almost always the same thing: I do not know how to get this right and I am afraid I am about to lose her. I have worked with enough men to know that the heat under the anger is grief.
You did not choose any of these. Your body chose.
You are now both inside states neither of you would have signed up for, trying to find a way back to each other across a room that has gone heavy.
This is the moment that decides what kind of relationship you are in. Not because of who is right. Because of what either of you knows how to do next.
Three things every man tries first. None of them work
All of them are well-intentioned.

The first is the immediate apology. You apologise before you have understood what you are apologising for. She can feel the apology is functional. It is not coming from contact with what she experienced. It is coming from the body wanting to switch off the alarm. The apology becomes another data point in the pattern: he says sorry, nothing changes, we keep ending up here.

The second is the over-explanation. You begin to explain what you meant. You walk her through your reasoning, your context, your intention. Some of this might be technically true. None of it is what her body is asking for. Her body is not asking for a defence. It is asking to be met where it is.

The third is the silence. You go quiet because nothing safe to say is coming, and you have learned that the wrong thing makes it worse. The silence reads, in her body, as withdrawal. The very thing she was already afraid of. Your absence becomes another rupture on top of the rupture.
None of this is your fault. You were never taught what to do here. There is no reason you would know.
Name the air. Stay. Invite, do not require
I am going to give you the structure that, in my hands, with more than 650 couples, has shifted this moment more than anything else I know.
It has three parts. None of them are clever.

One. Name the air. You stop trying to fix what just happened. You name that something has changed. Something just shifted between us. Or the air just changed. Or something landed for you. You do not interpret it. You do not assign blame. You name the fact of it. You give the room one shared piece of language for what just happened. Her body, which has been alone with what it just felt, now has a reference point.
This single move, on its own, has stopped countless escalations in front of me. The body softens when the thing it has been carrying alone is finally named by someone else.

Two. Stay. You do nothing for a moment. You do not move toward her physically unless your body is calm. You do not move away. You let your own body settle. You drop your shoulders. You take one slow breath that ends in a soft exhale. You let your face go open rather than braced.

What you are doing is offering her body a different reference point than the one it was tracking a moment ago. Mirror neurons mean that her body is reading yours all the way through this. If your body says we are still here, her body will start to register that before her mind can.

Three. Invite, do not require. Once you have named the air and let your body settle, you can ask one question. Not interrogating. Not fixing. Do you want to tell me what landed for you? Or simpler: I am here when you are ready.
The phrasing matters less than the absence of pressure. You are not requiring her to come back into language right now. You are letting her know that when she does, you will be there.

The window may be three minutes. It may be three days. Her body will tell her when it is safe to come back. The fastest way to extend that window is to make the room safe enough for the override not to kick in.
Fifteen seconds that changed nineteen years

I worked with a couple last year. He was a man who had spent most of his life being good in a crisis. Excellent in his career. Calm under pressure. Decisive. He had never figured out why none of these competencies seemed to land at home.
In our second session his wife said something difficult. She named a way she had felt invisible for several years. Her face changed. The room went heavy.
He started to do what he always did. Smooth it over. Reassure her. Make the moment more comfortable.
I asked him to stop.
I asked him to do three things. Notice that the air had changed. Stay in his own body. Wait.
He sat there for what he later told me felt like the longest fifteen seconds of his life.

His wife began to cry. Not the bracing kind of cry. The other kind. The cry that arrives when something that has been held alone for a long time is finally allowed to surface in front of someone who is not flinching.
He had never seen her cry like that. He had been married to her for nineteen years.
After she had cried for a few minutes, she looked at him. She said: I have not let myself feel that with you in a long time.
That was all. He did not have to fix anything. He did not have to apologise for anything. The repair had already happened in the staying.
Still following the breadcrumbs.Juliette

q: Where Still Following The Breadcrumbs Comes From

blocks.x: I normally just post twice a week on here. This one hit home, so it's coming to you today instead.
A week ago I found out that someone I've known for over fifteen years, a spiritual teacher, in one of my own communities, took her own life.
I'm not going to write about her here. That's not this piece, and it's not mine to write.
What I can't stop watching is us.
The tributes have been beautiful, some of them.
Underneath the tributes, the speculation has already started. The kind where people arrange the facts into a shape they can live with.
She taught shadow work. She was about to launch a new course.
Somehow, in the telling, it took her out. Like the work itself turned on her.
None of that is actually relevant. What I want to talk about is how we respond.
How someone can hold the most impactful work in a room and still not be held herself.
How we do that to our teachers, and how we do it to ourselves.
Part One: The Night I Was Fourteen
I was fourteen, maybe fifteen.
It brought me back to a night I haven't written about before.
I found my mother on her bed, comatose. A bottle of pills beside her. The phone still in her hand. On the other end, a woman was asking, in Dutch, "what's happening, what's happening?"
My mother had called an ambulance herself, then gone under before it arrived. Somehow the phone was still live, still in her fingers. This stranger's voice asking a question nobody was answering.
I don't fully know how I did what happened next.
I think I pulled her up by her hair. I got her into the car. I did not have a driver's licence, and you cannot legally drive in Holland until you're eighteen.
Somehow I drove her to the hospital and parked the car without crashing it. In that nervous system state, at that age, that's its own small miracle.
They rushed her in to have her stomach pumped.
Here's where it gets complicated.
I don't think bittersweet is even the right word for what's coming. Not for her. For me.

The man my mother was seeing, the affair, came to the hospital. My father was living abroad at the time, and my mother had given this man a key to our house. You make of that what you will, I certainly have my opinion about it.
He'd gone there, found the pills gone, worked out we weren't home, and started calling every hospital until he found us.
He came and found me in the waiting room. We hugged. We cried. His daughter was a friend of mine, which is its own strange detail to carry.
How complicated can life actually get?

He told my mother his wife wanted a divorce. It turned out she didn't. Her best friend had confronted my mother about the affair, at a dinner party we'd hosted. Driving home that night, my mother had been in tears, feeling betrayed.
Still, somehow, I was the one holding on to this man for whatever comfort he could give me in this moment of pain.
My mother's pain. Not mine, technically. Except it was entirely mine too, and there was nobody checking whose pain I was allowed to be in.
When my mother came to, in that hospital bed, she didn't see me. She only had eyes for him.
After a few minutes standing there I felt exactly what my partner Alex would call it now, decades later: "what am I, chopped liver?"
So I left. I drove the car back to my parents' house alone.
A friend was walking his dog past the house. Saw the lights on. Knocked on the window.
I burst into tears in his arms. He held me.
I want to stay with this a moment longer, because it matters more than a quick sentence can hold.
Being held, properly held, by someone who wasn't asking anything of me, undid something in me faster than words could have.
That was after a night where I'd been the one holding everyone. Physically hauling my own mother into a car.

It moved. The way held grief does. It moved from his arms into something else. Physical touch became sexual touch, and I let it. For a while there was real relief in that, a kind of relief I hadn't been offered anywhere else that night.
Afterwards I felt empty. Not ashamed exactly, though the shame arrived later, on schedule, the way it always does. Somebody, somewhere, would call that promiscuous.
I'd call it a fourteen-year-old's nervous system finding the fastest road out of a night it had no other way to survive. I'm not going to pretend I fully believe now that the road was wrong.

That's not unusual. Physical touch becomes sexual touch more often than any of us admit, especially in a state like that, wired open and hunting for release with nowhere else for it to go. That may be exactly what a body needs.
The judgement that lands afterwards is rarely about what actually happened. It's about the fact that you needed it that badly at all.

That's led me to something I still teach now, decades later: when you are wanting, more than anything, to be held by someone, that touch can still lead somewhere else entirely, and often that's exactly where the release happens.
I called my father at eight the next morning.
My father was abroad with my brother and his wife. My sister was studying abroad too.
There was no one. I didn't call anyone, because I didn't want to bother anyone.
That's what a third child does, sometimes. Doesn't bother anyone.
He came back immediately. Furious at my mother, and supporting her anyway, both at once.
Here's what I understand now about that night that I didn't understand then. It wasn't actually the beginning. It only felt like it.
It was the loudest version of a lesson I'd already learned, thirty years earlier, in a much smaller room.
Part Two: Where The Giving Started
I was four.
I gave my grandparent a drawing. I remember watching the whole room shift. The attention, the delight, the way a small thing I'd made rearranged the air around me.
Nobody sat me down and taught me the lesson. My body just filed it: giving something is what makes you matter. That's where the over-giving actually started.
The hospital, thirty years later, was the same imprint, at volume, on a night with far higher stakes than a piece of paper.

When you're a teenager and you're made to choose between your parents, when you're the one who cleans up the mess and drives the car and holds the phone, it doesn't teach you anything new. It just confirms, at full force, what a four-year-old already worked out with a crayon.
It doesn't imprint that you did something wrong. Everyone will tell you it wasn't your fault, and they're right. It doesn't matter, because that was never the imprint.
The imprint is quieter than that, and older than that. You learn that you matter, that you're important, by giving.
So you give. To show it. Over and over and over again….
Years later. My sister is dying.
I've watched myself do the same thing again since, in a completely different shape.

For a period, I was part of something called Unconditional Sex. An experiment, with someone, where the rule was simple and absolute: the moment the sensation left, whoever felt it leave said so, and we stopped.
No negotiation. That was the entire agreement.
What I learned from that rule mattered almost more than the sex did.

Most people assume a man would take an arrangement like that and be grateful for it. Some were. A real number of them, the moment I said stop, tried to keep going anyway, tried to talk me back into it, tried to make sure they still got what they'd come for.
The ones who didn't, who actually stopped the second I said it, taught me more about what safety in a body feels like than any training I'd paid for.

Underneath all of it, the truthful reason I was there at all: it was how I got my relief during a year I could not otherwise bear. My sister was dying, and I did not have language for that pain. So my body found a door instead.
Was it soothing. Was it bypassing. Was it simply the body doing the one thing bodies know how to do with unbearable feeling: move it, however it can, wherever the door is open.
I still don't fully know the answer. I'm not sure it needs one.
Part Three: Back To Now
I've worked with mothers whose daughters took their own lives.
I worked with a mother who had to offer her own baby as a sacrifice inside a cult. How does anyone come back from that.
I have been shown, myself, what it looks like to be offered a portal out of this life. An actual way to step out of the 3-D world we're living in. Every single time, something has brought me back.
My children. The thought of what they'd feel.
To say we understand what happens in someone's mind when they're shown a portal like that, and they take it, is arrogant. I won't pretend to.
This week, in my body.
I want to name what's actually happening physically, because it's stranger than grief usually gets described as.
I've known her fifteen years. In all that time, I don't think I've mentioned her to Alex more than once or twice, in passing.
Alex said to me this week, "I've never seen you like this."
Tearful. Thinking about her constantly. My legs finding their way up onto a chair at ninety degrees before I've even decided to put them there.
A death that distant should not be doing this to a body. Except trauma doesn't file things by how close you were to someone. It files them by what they touch.
Bessel van der Kolk's line gets quoted so often it's turned into a slogan, so let me say it as the plain fact it actually is: the body keeps the score.

A nervous system that once hauled a comatose parent into a car and drove her to a hospital at fourteen does not forget that it can happen again. It waits, filed away, for the next thing that rhymes with it.
Someone who held everyone, not being held by anyone. That's the rhyme. My body found it before my mind caught up.
That's why I'm lying flat on my back most days this week, legs up on a chair at ninety degrees.
It's a message to my nervous system more than a stretch. There's no need to run, because a body braced to run doesn't put its legs up for anyone.
That's why I'm doing cross-body movement. Right hand to left knee, left hand to right knee, slow, over and over.

Crossing the midline like that is one of the oldest tricks a body has for moving a stuck charge out of itself, the same physics underneath EMDR's alternating stimulation, though what I'm doing isn't EMDR. A body processes what's stuck sideways more easily than it processes it head-on.
That's why I'm shaking. Actually shaking, hands and arms, when I lie there.
Animals do this after a threat passes, and most humans clamp down on it, because a shaking adult looks alarming to everyone watching.
Peter Levine spent decades studying that clamp-down. What he found is that the shake is the discharge, the nervous system completing something it didn't get to complete at fourteen.
I'm not stopping mine.
Part Four: The Actual Breadcrumbs
I crossed 35,000 followers on Instagram today. I thought that number would feel like a straightforward good day.
Instead I've been tearful, and proud, in the same hour. I've had to learn something in real time, AGAIN: those two are not in competition.
A body can hold a milestone and a grief at once, and it doesn't need you to pick one and perform it convincingly…. right?!
My brand is called Feel Fully You. That's not a tagline. It's the actual promise…. and man oh man, have I grown into that brand, through thick and thin…
There's a particular irony in having to decide, on a Thursday I didn't plan for, whether I'm actually willing to do that in public…. be vulnerable, be real, show ALL pieces of me.

I built a business on the promise that the felt experience is the honest one, and today that promise came due. I'm paying it, tearful, shaking, thumb to forefinger, in front of anyone who wants to watch.
I'm writing about it and speaking it out loud too. That's its own kind of moving it through, and it's the only reason this piece exists at all.
Looking back at all of it. The drawing at four. The hospital at fourteen.
The man, the friend with the dog. The years with Unconditional Sex while my sister was dying.
I don't see a woman who kept making the same mistake.
I see the actual breadcrumbs.
Every one of those was my body finding its own way through something no one had given me a map for. It's exactly why I teach what I teach now.
This is what it actually means, every single day, to keep following the breadcrumbs.
Still following the breadcrumbs.Juliette

q: Why Am I The Only One Who Notices What Needs Doing?

blocks.x: Nobody in your house voted for you to be the one who knows where the spare uniform is.

Nobody sat down and decided, out loud, that you'd be the one tracking the sizes, the appointments, the group chat, the fact that you're out of the thing you didn't know you were nearly out of until you were. It just became you. Somewhere along the way, that started to feel like a verdict on your character instead of what it actually is: an unmade decision that defaulted to whoever was paying attention first.
Part One: Noticing was never divided
The noticing is what exhausts you. Plenty of the physical tasks get shared now, more evenly than a generation ago. What doesn't get shared is the noticing itself.

The knowing something needs doing before it's been said out loud. The holding of forty small threads at once, so that nothing drops. This lives in your nervous system, permanently, running in the background, whether or not anything is actually happening in front of you right now.

Your partner can do every dish in the house and still never once have to ask himself what's for dinner tomorrow, or why the mood in the car this morning felt off. Those questions live in you, running, whether you're at your desk, in a meeting, or lying next to him at midnight.

Here's what I'm actually seeing in the couples I work with. He genuinely wants to help. He asks what he can do. That question, well meant as it is, hands the thinking straight back to her, because now she has to notice the gap, translate it into a task, and hand it to him in a form he can execute. The asking becomes one more thing on the list she's already running.

He's often working exactly as hard as she is, just in a different current, episodic instead of constant. The car service every six months. The nine hundred small things a household needs today, just to stay upright, that's her current.
Sociologists have started giving this a name, the mental load, but the phrase undersells it. It's the operating system underneath every other task, invisible exactly because it works.

One real study, out of the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne, found mothers were carrying 71% of the household tasks that take real mental effort, tracking when things run out, when things need attention before they become unmissable. Fathers, on average, carried more of what researchers call episodic labour, the things that happen occasionally and get remembered because they're rare, not because they're constant.
One researcher on that team, Leah Ruppaner, put it plainly: “You don't bring your dishes to work with you, but you bring this everywhere.”
Part Two: Give the noticing a place to land, not just the task
You cannot fix an invisible, unbounded, permanently running load by asking your partner to do more chores. You already knew that. It's why asking him to help more has never actually worked for long.
What actually redistributes it is fifteen minutes, one prompt, and a structure that makes it safe for both of you to actually hear the answer.
Try this. The Dyad.
Set a timer. Fifteen minutes. One of you reads the prompt out loud:
“TELL ME WHAT I CAN DO TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD. WHAT DO YOU NEED ME TO DO?”
The other answers. One honest, succinct answer, not the whole list at once.

The listener can only say one of three things back, nothing else. “Thank you.” if you've understood it, that's the only response that closes the round and passes the turn. “Clarify that.” if you haven't, and the speaker keeps going on the same thread. “Summarise that.” if the answer's getting long, you reflect back what you heard, the speaker corrects you or nods, and keeps going. Neither of those passes the turn. Only “thank you” does.

Once the turn passes, you swap. Same prompt, the other person answers now, going deeper than the first pass. Back and forth, same one prompt, the whole fifteen minutes, each round pulling a little further down than the last.

None of this is guesswork. Partners who hold hands under real threat show a measurably lower stress response in the brain, strongest in the relationships already running well. Ease without an agenda calms a nervous system. Pressure, even well meant, reads as one more thing to defend against.
No fixing. No defending. No agreeing or disagreeing. You do not have to like what you hear. You only have to understand it.

Here's what I'm actually seeing in the couples who've done this with me. Fifteen minutes in, on one prompt, they understand what the other one actually needs, properly, not the version they'd already assumed. Once that's landed, dividing up the actual tasks stops being a negotiation. It's just obvious.
Do this once a week. The structure is what does the work, not the specific prompt.

One more thing that actually works. Once you both know what needs holding, name a whole category, not a task: “school admin is yours now, start to finish, I'm not the backup.” A category means he has to build his own noticing for it, not borrow yours.
Part Three: What changes
Nothing changes the week you start this. A system that's run one way for years takes longer than a week to rewire, that's simply how long it takes.
What changes, weeks in, is smaller than you'd expect. He starts a category and doesn't ask you where things are kept for it. He stops asking what he can do and starts just noticing on his own.
Nobody sits down and votes on it happening, either. He just starts knowing where the spare uniform is too, unprompted, and you notice you've stopped checking whether he remembered.
Both of you are running a pattern, learned early, running still.
Yours has a name: Holder. You notice everyone, you got fluent in everyone else's needs before your own, because your nervous system learned early that being needed was safer than being wanted.

His has a name too: Operator. He solves problems, makes decisions, keeps moving, when life needs handling, he handles it. Somewhere along the way, doing became the only feeling he trusted. Which is exactly why naming the category works on him. Operators don't need to be asked to notice. They need something concrete handed to them to go and handle, and they'll handle it completely.
You're both just running the pattern you learned. Now you both have a name for it.

q: Why Do I Feel Disgusted When He Touches Me?

blocks.x: You are standing at the sink and his hand arrives on your lower back, and something in you pulls away so fast you have to hold still to cover it.
He means it kindly. That is the part that undoes you.

Then the second wave lands, about a second and a half behind the first, and it is the worse of the two. The recoil you could almost live with. It is the shame arriving on top of it that keeps you awake.
Because you love him. Nothing has happened. He has done nothing except put a warm hand on his partner's back at half past nine on a Tuesday.
So at one in the morning, phone tilted away from him, you type the sentence you would never say out loud: why do I feel disgusted when he touches me?
Part One: A flinch and this are two different animals
A flinch is fast. Something moves at the edge of your vision, your shoulder jumps, and four seconds later you are fine and slightly embarrassed. Startle comes and goes.
What you are describing does not go. It arrives with the touch, it spreads, it has a taste to it, and it leaves a residue that lasts the rest of the evening.
It also carries something a flinch never does. A moral flavour. A sense that the wrongness is somehow yours.
Disgust was built as a rejection response, the body's way of saying this does not come in. Fear makes you run. Disgust makes you expel.

It began with food and rot and contamination, then got recruited for anything the body decided must be kept out. Paul Rozin spent a career mapping how far it travels once it is off the leash. It stops being about spoiled meat quite quickly, and attaches to people, to touch, to whole categories of contact.
Disgust is the last move your body makes. It has already tried everything quieter.

Your body says no in an order, and the order is quiet at the start. First there is a stillness that nobody sees, including you. A very small withholding, a fraction of breath held, a two-degree drop in something you have no name for.
If that gets read, it never escalates. Most of the time it does not get read, often because you were the one who trained yourself not to send it clearly.
So it goes up a rung. You turn slightly. You reach for the tea towel. You start a sentence about the bins.
When that gets missed too, month after month, year after year, the body stops spending energy on signals that never worked. It goes straight to the biggest lever it has left.

It picks the one response you cannot talk yourself out of. That is the whole design. You can override a subtle no. You can push through a turned shoulder. Nobody has ever reasoned themselves out of revulsion.
Your body is using the only language that has ever produced a result.
Part Two: The next forty minutes
So ask the question you have not been asking at one in the morning.
When his hand lands on your back at half nine, what is your body actually responding to?
The hand weighs about half a kilo. It is warm. On its own it is almost nothing.
Your body is responding to the next forty minutes it has learned to expect from that hand.

This is what runs underneath most of what I see. When touch has meant one thing for long enough, the body stops processing contact and starts processing the sequence. The hand becomes an opening move in a transaction whose ending is already known.
So it braces at the whole arc, arriving at once, compressed into the second the palm lands.
He puts a hand on you meaning I love you, and your nervous system receives here we go again, and both of you are being completely truthful about what just happened.

Stephen Porges gave this appraisal a name, neuroception, the body's continuous reading of safety and threat running well below anything you consciously decide. Your body finished its read while his hand was still in the air.
Everything you have ever been sold is aimed at making you want it more. Lingerie. Weekends away. Trying harder.
I have almost never seen wanting be the thing that was stuck.
A body with its foot flat on the brake needs to find out what it is braking for.

There is one pattern I see this run through more than any other. I call it the Armour. It contains in order to stay safe, and its particular signature is that softness feels dangerous where pressure does not.
Women in the Armour can often manage brisk, functional, sexual touch far better than they can manage tenderness. A hand held gently for too long is unbearable in a way that nothing rough ever is.
One client put it more clearly than I ever have. “Day 1 you had me bawling… softness and slow touch is triggering… I started crying immediately.”
If that sentence made something in you go very quiet, you already know which pattern you are running.
Part Three: What actually moves it
Three things do not work, and you have probably tried all three.

Pushing through. You let it happen and you go somewhere else while it does. Every time you do that you teach your body that its biggest signal changes nothing, and next time it must come in louder or earlier. Performing costs you capacity you are going to need later.

Explaining it to him in the moment. His hand is still on you, you are flooded, and now you are trying to construct a sentence that does not detonate. It will come out as a verdict on him. He will hear one.

Waiting for it to pass. This is the one I would happily go to war over. You have been sold the idea that desire is spontaneous, that it will simply return if you are patient and the conditions are right. It does not come back on its own, because nothing has changed about what your body is predicting. Every month of waiting is another month of rehearsing the same forecast.
What does move it is smaller and far less romantic than any of that.
You take the destination off the table, out loud, for a fixed period.
Six weeks, and both of you know it in advance. Nothing is allowed to lead anywhere, and that is the entire instruction.
Once the body stops predicting the arc, a hand goes back to being a hand. It can be assessed on its own terms instead of on years of forecast.

The furthest I have seen this go was a woman who had been sexually assaulted and had no memory of it. Her partner did not know how to approach her, or touch her, or be near her, without her body closing.
He kept reaching. She kept going somewhere else. He was certain he was doing it wrong.
He was doing everything right. Her body simply did not know that yet.

We spent a day together. I showed him how to hold still. How to approach. How to ground himself so that she could feel his stillness from where she was, and decide, on her own timing, whether to move towards it.
He stopped arriving with a destination attached, and her body had something it could read.
Ropes, as containment. A raspberry on her tongue. A silk blindfold. Her partner whispering good girl.
She felt herself again.
Here is what to expect if you start.

It gets louder before it gets quieter. A body that has been overridden for years will, given a genuine opening, tell you the size of the backlog all at once. The client I quoted earlier was crying on day one, over exactly this. Nothing has gone wrong when that happens. That is a channel opening after a long time shut.

Then the disgust starts arriving with information attached. It stops being one solid wall and gets specific. That hand, at that hour, with that thing behind it. Specific is workable. Specific can be asked about, and asked for differently.
Neutrality is the last thing to come back, and it is the cherry on top. A hand lands on you and it is just a hand. Nothing more. Nothing less.

For months you have read the recoil at the sink as evidence about the state of your love for him. It has been asking for something for a very long time, in the only language it had left, and nothing has answered it yet.
Your body braced. Patterns can be changed.

q: Why Do I Feel Guilty The Second I Stop Moving?

blocks.x: Katarina is a dermatologist. Deeply respected in her field, she knows more about the body, professionally, than almost anyone I've ever worked with.
(Enough changed here to protect her privacy. The pattern isn't changed at all.)
She came to me having gone on and on and on, the way capable people do, for years, until her nervous system simply couldn't hold the line any longer. She had to take time off work. Completely.
She could explain exactly what stress does to skin, to cortisol, to the body's whole chemistry. She had never once been taught how to actually live inside her own.
That's exactly where it starts.
Part One: What you've started calling normal
“I just have a lot on at the moment.”
“I've always been like this.”
“I'm not tired, I'm fine, I just need a coffee.”
Every one of those is a body that adapted so long ago it forgot it was adapting.
For years you keep functioning. Meeting deadlines. Managing the house. Being there for whoever needs it, partner, kids, the friend who calls at the wrong time and stays on the phone anyway.

What goes unnoticed is everything underneath that. The thinking, anticipating, remembering, checking. Sociologists call this emotional labour. That undersells it. It's a constant, standing state of responsibility, an ongoing tally of what needs doing and what might go wrong if you stop checking.

Your body learns this the way it learns anything, through repetition. It learns that vigilance keeps things from dropping. It learns that staying half-braced is cheaper than being caught off guard. It learns that stillness is when things go wrong, so it simply stops fully arriving at stillness at all.
Most people picture burnout as collapse. Someone who can't get out of bed. Someone visibly, obviously not okay.

What it actually looks like, most of the time, at first, is the most competent person in the room. The one who never drops the ball. The one everyone assumes is fine, because fine is the only setting you've ever shown anyone.
Functioning and actually being well are two different things entirely, and mistaking one for the other is how this goes unnoticed for years.

The shoulders that never fully drop, even asleep. The jaw you catch yourself clenching in traffic, in meetings, in the two minutes before anyone else wakes up. Rest that doesn't touch anything, because stillness has never once been safe.
You've gotten so skilled at carrying this that you stopped registering the weight of it. Your body kept its own record anyway.

She'd stopped being able to slow down long enough to notice she needed to. That's what took her out of work in the end, not one crisis, just years of a nervous system running in the red until it simply stopped complying.
When I asked her the last time she'd done anything with no purpose attached to it, nothing to fix, nothing to optimise, she genuinely could not remember.

The same vigilance that keeps you scanning for what needs doing is the exact same setting your body uses for touch, for rest, for someone's hand landing on you with nothing attached to it. Your nervous system doesn't run two separate systems, one for managing everything and one for receiving affection. It runs one. Braced. Once braced becomes the default for keeping things from dropping, it becomes the default for everything else too, including the people who want nothing from you at all.

Here's what I'm actually seeing in the women who come to me. They don't usually say they're burnt out. They say they don't know how to relax, even on holiday. They say their partner keeps offering to help and they keep saying they've got it. They say they can't remember the last time a hand landed on them without their body already working out what it owed back.
Part Two: What actually starts undoing it
One. Notice what you've started calling normal.

Ask yourself, honestly: what have I started calling “just how I am”? A clenched jaw. Never sitting down without your phone already in your hand. Interrupted sleep you've stopped mentioning to anyone. Name it. You can't undo what you won't first call by its name.
Two. Build the recovery in. Don't wait to deserve it.

Something today, not the holiday you're saving it for. Try Touch Base®: thumb to forefinger, one breath in, one breath out. Less time than the kettle takes to boil. Hand resting in your lap, nothing to organise, nothing to prepare for whoever needs you next.
Three. Ask the question before you act on the thought.

Not every thought that lands in your head at 9pm needs you to get up and do something about it. Try asking, before you move: does this need me right now? Most of the time the honest answer is no. You'll do it anyway the first fifty times you ask. That's fine. The question is the practice, not the answer.
Do all three for two weeks before you decide whether it's working.
Part Three: What actually changes
Nothing, the first week. A system built over years doesn't rewire itself in seven days.

Weeks in, something smaller than you'd expect. A hand lands on your shoulder and you don't catalogue what you owe for it. You sit down before the list is finished and your body doesn't punish you for it three hours later.

For Katarina, the thing that actually moved it was small enough to feel almost silly. She started standing in front of her own mirror, looking herself in the eyes, and saying it out loud: “I love you.” Some mornings she wrote it across the glass in lipstick, so it was still there the next time she looked.
Small. Almost embarrassing, she told me, the first few times.

Her body had spent years being told, in a thousand indirect ways, that it mattered only for what it could do next. A woman looking her own reflection in the eye and meaning it is a different instruction entirely, and her nervous system took it in the way it takes in anything repeated enough: as evidence.
Katarina's pattern has a name. So does yours, almost certainly, whether it looks like hers or not.
She's what I call a Holder. Give to stay connected, that's the shorthand. The one who keeps holding, holding, holding, until the body puts something down whether she agreed to it or not.
Once she had a name for it, she had something to actually work with.
One evening, a hand lands on your shoulder, and you don't immediately catalogue what it's going to cost you. You just let it stay there a moment longer than you would have a year ago.

q: Why Do I Feel Like I Have To Fake Calm In Front Of My Kids?

blocks.x: Your daughter falls off the step, looks fine for exactly one second, then looks at your face before she decides whether to cry.
This is her whole nervous system, working exactly the way it's supposed to.

Researchers call it social referencing. In one of the studies behind it, one-year-olds crawled toward what looked like a sudden drop in the floor, a visual cliff, perfectly safe, an optical trick, and stopped right at the edge. Almost every single one of them looked at their mother's face before deciding what to do next. If she smiled, they crossed. If her face showed fear, none of them did.
Before they can talk, children are already reading you for the real answer. Not your words. Your face.
Part One: What they're actually reading
They're not reading whether you're calm. They're reading whether your face and your words agree.
“You're fine, sweetheart” said with a soft, easy mouth lands as exactly that: fine.
“You're fine, sweetheart” said through a tight jaw, held eyes, a mouth that isn't matching the words, lands as something else entirely. Danger, dressed as reassurance.

Two signals specifically. The muscles around the eyes, the real ones that only fire in a genuine smile, not the ones you can move on command. And the jaw, which tightens the moment a body starts preparing for a threat, whether or not that threat is real, whether or not you've said a single word about it.
A child can't name either of those things. Their body reads them anyway, every time, faster than thought.

Here's what I'm actually seeing in the mothers who come to me. They think the job is staying calm. Actually calm, all the way through, every single time. So when they can't, when the face slips, when the jaw gives them away, they read it as a failure to hide better next time.
That's the wrong job entirely.

Elena came to me certain she was doing lasting damage to her son every time he caught her looking stressed. She'd started rehearsing her face in the car before she walked in the door. A whole performance, before the door even opened.
I asked her what she thought her son needed from her. “To always feel safe,” she said. “To never see me rattled.”

Real safety gets built differently. Children develop their own capacity to recover from a rupture by watching someone else recover from one, out loud, close up. That's the actual mechanism, backed by decades of attachment research, not the performance Elena had been rehearsing in her car.

Psychologist Edward Tronick spent decades studying exactly this moment, the still-face and its repair. A parent goes flat, unresponsive, just for a moment. The baby visibly struggles. Then the parent softens, re-engages, and something happens that matters more than the flat moment ever did: the coming back.

This isn't only about the moments something goes wrong. I watched a video recently by Pastor Blackwood, yes, that's his real name, his parents actually called him Pastor, teaching his eight-month-old to pull himself upright, ropes, thick mats, elastic bands rigged up like a proper little gym. The baby fell, tried again, fell again.

What actually held my attention was the father. Steady. Present. Not once gripping, hovering, or bracing on his son's behalf, so the baby never had to either. He got up, using his jaw, his arms, his legs, everything, and the joy on his face when he held himself upright, arms still shaking, was enormous.

Some of the comments under that video called it showing off. I saw a man regulated enough to let his son struggle in front of him without needing to rescue him from the struggle itself. That's proprioception being built in real time, the body learning where it is in space, and it only gets built when someone steady is close enough to make the falling safe.
Part Two: The two-second repair
You cannot manufacture a face your child can't read. Don't try. That's the performance that's actually exhausting you, and it was never the job.
Try this. The repair, not the mask.
The moment you catch your own face doing the thing, the tight mouth, the flat eyes, the jaw, don't fix it. Let your child see it land, then repair it, out loud, within a few seconds.
Soften your breath first. One slow exhale, longer than the breath in.
Let your voice follow it down. Slower, warmer, even just slightly.
A hand on their back, or your own chest, whichever is closer.
Then say the true thing, plainly: “I got a fright there. I'm okay now.”
That whole sequence takes less time than it took you to read this paragraph. It lets them watch what happens next.
Part Three: What it actually teaches them
What it actually teaches them: recovery.

Every time your child watches your face go tight and then watches you come back from it, out loud, close up, they're learning something far more useful than unshakeable: a hard moment ends. A body can come back. This is survivable, because they just watched someone do it, close enough to touch.

q: Why Do I Feel Nothing When My Partner Touches Me?

blocks.x: He puts his hand on the small of your back, and you feel the weight of it, the warmth of it, and nothing else.
You used to feel that hand in your knees. Tonight it lands like a coat someone has draped over your shoulders. Registered. Filed. No charge.
You lie there afterwards running the maths on the last time you actually wanted it, and you cannot find the date.
So you ask the internet the thing you cannot ask him: what is wrong with me?
Part One: Your desire did not leave. Your capacity ran out.
The internet gives you two answers, and both read like a sentence. Your hormones have gone. Or you have fallen out of love and should leave.
I have spent fifteen years with women in exactly this, and it is almost never either one.
Here is what nobody names. Your body has a window, a range it can stay present and feel inside. Stress, exhaustion, years of bracing all shrink that window until there is barely any room left in it.

When touch arrives at the edge of a window narrowed to a slit, your body does the only intelligent thing left. It checks out. It goes numb because feeling has become more than it can hold right now, even though nothing in you is truly gone.
You know the signs, even without names for them.
You brace a half-second before he touches you. You leave your body during sex and plan tomorrow's list. You perform relaxed at dinner while something in you stands guard.
That is a nervous system with no spare capacity, protecting you the only way it knows. It was never a low sex drive.
Desire cannot move into a body that has no room. First you make room.
Part Two: Start smaller than you think. Tonight.
Here is what makes it worse. The weekend away. The lingerie. The big date night you are both secretly hoping fixes it.
You are asking a body with a slit of a window to throw the doors open. It cannot, so it braces harder, and you both go to bed quietly defeated, more certain something is wrong.
The way back is the opposite of a grand gesture. You go so small it feels almost silly.
Try this tonight. Not sex. Not even the promise of it.

Ask him for three minutes of touch that is not allowed to lead anywhere. A hand on your arm. Your back stroked. You are not performing, not reciprocating, not managing his experience. You receive, and that is all.

While he does it, do one thing with your attention. Do not chase whether it feels sexy. Notice what your body is literally doing. Not "this is nice." The plain physical facts. Warmth here. Tightness there. A flutter. A held breath. A wanting to pull away.
That last one counts too. If your body wants to flinch, let it, and notice that.

This is the whole move, and it is smaller than anyone tells you. You are teaching a guarded body that a hand can land and ask for nothing. Three minutes, then stop on purpose, while it still feels safe. Tomorrow, three minutes again.
You are not trying to feel desire. You are widening the window desire can walk back through.
Most women have never been shown what comes next, so let me take you all the way in, to how the feeling actually comes back online, in the order the body does it.

q: Why Do I Pull Away When He Hugs Me?

blocks.x: He comes up behind you at the kettle and puts both arms around you, and you are out of them before you have decided anything.
Your body did that. You watched it happen.
There is a half second afterwards where you are both standing there. He says something light so neither of you has to name it. You say something light back.
Then you spend the rest of the evening doing the arithmetic. He has done nothing. You love him. You have loved him through considerably worse than a hug.
So at one in the morning, with the room dark and him asleep beside you, you type the thing you cannot say at the kettle: why do I pull away when he hugs me?
Part One: The skin changed
Oestrogen runs your skin too. Properly, measurably, with biopsies behind it.

Skin collagen tracks how long it has been since your last period rather than how old you are. Roughly a third of it goes in the first five years. Then about two percent a year for the fifteen after that. Brincat and Studd took biopsies from sixty-nine women in 1987 and the finding has held up ever since.
Oestrogen receptors sit right through the skin, densest in the face, the legs and the genitals. As oestrogen drops the barrier gets leakier and holds less water.
So the surface his hand lands on is a different surface from the one he was landing on five years ago. Read that again, because it is the whole thing.

Here is what I watch in the women who come to me around this. They describe the change as though it happened to their feelings. They tell me they have gone cold, that something in them has switched off, that they are worried they do not love him anymore. When we slow down and get specific about what actually happens in the two seconds after contact, it is almost always happening at the level of skin, and nervous system, and what the body has learned to expect.

I want to be straight with you about what kind of evidence that is. The skin research is solid. The research on how touch is registered as we age is also solid. Nobody has joined those two up and studied it properly in menopausal women. So what I am handing you is what I watch happen in the room, over and over, with no citation sitting behind it. You should know which of those two you are being given.
Part Two: The hug was never the thing
A hug is about fifteen seconds. On its own it is almost nothing.
Your body is responding to everything those fifteen seconds have come to mean.

If sex has been hurting, and for an enormous number of women it has, your body has been running a pain forecast for a while now. The international consultation on this in 2024 put painful sex somewhere between twenty and seventy-eight percent, which tells you both how common it is and how badly it has been studied.

What happens next is well established. Pain produces watchfulness. Watchfulness produces tension, including in the pelvic floor. That tension increases the pain. Round and round. Then the body stops waiting for the painful moment at all and starts backing away from the whole context around it.
That much is documented for genital pain. Whether it reaches all the way out to a pair of arms at the kettle, nobody has studied.
I watch it reach.
His arms arrive meaning I love you. Your nervous system receives here we go again. Both of those are true accounts of the same fifteen seconds.

Then there is the sleep. Up to four in five women are getting hot flushes through this, three in five are losing their nights to them. A body that has not slept properly since March has less of everything available to it. Tolerance for being touched is one of the first things to go.
There is something else, and it is about him.

When researchers looked at what happens to women's relationships across the menopause transition, friendships largely survived it. Partners did not fare nearly as well. The paper says outright that the relational side of this is badly understudied. What I notice, in my own room, is how little these women expect anyone to understand it. There is rarely any anger in that. They have just stopped expecting anyone to come.

He is walking into completely different weather every day with no forecast. He cannot see the skin change. He cannot see the pain forecast. He gets one piece of information, which is that his arms are not wanted, and he draws the only conclusion available to him.
So he stops reaching. Then you have the distance as well as everything else.

I remember the exact session where this clicked into place for me, watching a woman mid-sentence stop trusting her own account of what was happening. She kept saying, “I still love him, so why does this feel so wrong,” turning the question over like there had to be an answer in there she was missing.

We slowed the whole thing down to the actual seconds. Not the story about the relationship, not the meaning she'd built around it. Just what her body did, in real time, when his arm landed on her shoulder at the counter that morning. The felt sense.
And there it was: a genuine physiological event, arriving faster than any thought about him could, nothing to do with how she felt about him at all.

That's the moment I stopped treating this as a relationship pattern women bring me and started treating it as a body one. Once you can see the actual mechanism, the guilt she'd been carrying for months, convinced she'd stopped loving him, has somewhere real to go instead of nowhere at all.
Part Three: Where to start when your skin says no

You already know that pushing through does not work. You have tried it. Every time you let it happen and go somewhere else while it does, you teach your body that its signal changed nothing, so next time it arrives earlier and louder.
What moves this is smaller and much less romantic than anything you have been sold.
Two practices, whole, free, both from my own bank. Start tonight.
The Breath Bridge. This one asks nothing at all of your skin, which is exactly why it goes first.
Sit facing each other. Close enough to feel the warmth coming off him, not touching. Breathe four in, hold for two, six out. Three minutes on a timer.
When the timer goes, one word each. Then you stop.

It is written as a monthly one. Most people are surprised by it, because it turns out you can be that intimate without a single hand landing anywhere. If touch is currently the thing you are dreading, this is the rung that is actually available to you tonight.
The Three Breath Hold. For the moments one of you is underwater.
Reach for his hand. Do not speak. Three slow breaths together, in through the nose, out through the mouth.
That is the whole thing. Held in silence rather than solved. No fixing, no discussion, nothing required afterwards, and crucially nothing that leads anywhere. A hand is allowed to be only a hand.

The reason both of these work is the same reason. Neither one is going anywhere. Once your body stops predicting the arc, it can assess what is actually happening instead of what happened the last four times.
Here is what to expect if you start.

It gets louder before it gets quieter. A body that has been overridden for a long time will, given a genuine opening, tell you the size of the backlog all at once. Nothing has gone wrong when that happens.

Then it gets specific. The pulling away stops being one solid wall and starts arriving with information attached. That kind of contact, at that hour, with that behind it. Specific is workable. Specific can be asked about, and asked for differently.

For months the kettle has been standing in as evidence about whether you still love him, while your body has been speaking something smaller and far more physical the whole time, in the only language it has left, and nothing has answered it yet.
Being touched isn't the same as feeling touch. Patterns can be changed.
